headline: Motion is change in position over time—and once started, it tends to continue
universal_truth: What's in motion stays in motion; starting is harder than continuing; momentum carries you
fun_facts: Earth is moving at 67,000 mph around the sun—you don't feel it because everything around you moves with it
The fastest human sprint speed recorded is about 27 mph (Usain Bolt)
Even 'stationary' objects on Earth are moving through space at incredible speeds
discussion_questions: What's in motion in your life right now?
What's stuck that you wish was moving?
How do you maintain momentum on long projects?

hook.script: You're moving right now. Earth spins at 1,000 mph. It orbits the sun at 67,000 mph. The solar system moves through the galaxy. There is no absolute stillness—only motion relative to other motion. Everything moves.

cliff.script: We think of stillness as natural and motion as requiring effort. But physics says otherwise. What's the natural state of things?
cliff.prompt: What's the natural state of objects?

options.text: Objects naturally maintain their current state—if moving, they continue moving; if still, they stay still—until a force changes them
options.response: Yes. This is Newton's First Law—inertia. Motion doesn't require constant pushing. Starting and stopping require force; continuing does not.

options.text: Things naturally slow down and stop
options.response: That's what we observe, but only because friction applies force—in space, things coast forever...

fact1.title: Inertia
fact1.script: Objects resist change. A heavy object is hard to start moving—and hard to stop. This resistance to change is inertia. It's not laziness; it's physics. Changing state always requires overcoming inertia.

fact2.title: Momentum Carries
fact2.script: Once moving, motion tends to continue. This is why starting a habit is harder than maintaining one. Why interrupted projects are hard to restart. Momentum is real—use it.

fact3.title: Small Starts Count
fact3.script: The hardest part is starting. Once moving, much less force maintains motion than started it. This is why tiny first steps matter—they overcome initial inertia. Motion creates more motion.

wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: What's in motion stays in motion. Starting is harder than continuing. Create momentum, then ride it.

outro.script: That's Day 222. Tomorrow, we'll explore speed—how fast things go. Until then, start something small and let momentum build.

growTrack.title: Momentum Start - Tiny First Step
growTrack.activity: Pick something you've been meaning to start. Take the smallest possible first step today—not a full effort, just motion. Open the document. Send one email. Do one pushup. The goal is motion, not completion. Motion creates momentum.
